knowledge_point.title: Integrating a Linear Rational Function and Simplifying the Arbitrary Constant

question.:question/problem: Calculate $\int \frac{1}{3-4x}\,\text{d}x.$ Assume that $K$ is an arbitrary positive constant.
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, let $u=3-4x.$ Then differentiating with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-4\,⟹\,\text{d}x=-\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u.
$$

We can now rewrite the integral in terms of $u,$ solve it, and write the final answer in terms of $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{3-4x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot (-\frac{1}{4})\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡|3-4x|+C\end{aligned}
$$

We can further simplify the above by writing $C=-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡K$ for another arbitrary constant $K,$ and then we can combine the two terms using the laws of logarithms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡|3-4x|+C & =-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡|3-4x|-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡K \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}(\operatorname{ln}⁡|3-4x|+\operatorname{ln}⁡K) \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|3-4x|)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we finally conclude that

$$
\int \frac{1}{3-4x}\text{d}x=-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|3-4x|).
$$

generation.domain: x real excluding 3/4; K>0; C arbitrary real on each connected interval

question.:question/problem: Calculate $\int \frac{1}{6x+2}\,\text{d}x.$ Assume that $K$ is an arbitrary positive constant.
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, let $u=6x+2.$ Then differentiating with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=6\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{6}\text{d}u.
$$

We can now rewrite the integral in terms of $u,$ solve it, and write the final answer in terms of $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{6x+2}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{6}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡|6x+2|+C\end{aligned}
$$

We can further simplify the above by writing $C=\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡K$ for another arbitrary constant $K,$ and then we can combine the two terms using the laws of logarithms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡|6x+2|+C & =\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡|6x+2|+\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡K \\  & =\frac{1}{6}(\operatorname{ln}⁡|6x+2|+\operatorname{ln}⁡K) \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|6x+2|)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we finally conclude that

$$
\int \frac{1}{6x+2}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|6x+2|).
$$

question.:question/problem: Calculate $\int \frac{6}{5-5x}\,\text{d}x.$ Assume that $K$ is an arbitrary positive constant.
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, let $u=5-5x.$ Then differentiating with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-5\,⟹\,\text{d}x=-\frac{1}{5}\text{d}u.
$$

We can now rewrite the integral in terms of $u,$ solve it, and write the final answer in terms of $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{6}{5-5x}\,\text{d}x & =6\int \frac{1}{5-5x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =6\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot (-\frac{1}{5})\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{6}{5}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{6}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =-\frac{6}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡|5-5x|+C\end{aligned}
$$

We can further simplify the above by writing $C=-\frac{6}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡K$ for another arbitrary constant $K,$ and then we can combine the two terms using the laws of logarithms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{6}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡|5-5x|+C & =-\frac{6}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡|5-5x|-\frac{6}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡K \\  & =-\frac{6}{5}(\operatorname{ln}⁡|5-5x|+\operatorname{ln}⁡K) \\  & =-\frac{6}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|5-5x|)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we finally conclude that

$$
\int \frac{6}{5-5x}\,\text{d}x=-\frac{6}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|5-5x|).
$$

question.:question/problem: Calculate $\int \frac{5}{3x+6}\,\text{d}x.$ Assume that $K$ is an arbitrary positive constant.
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, let $u=3x+6.$ Then differentiating with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u.
$$

We can now rewrite the integral in terms of $u,$ solve it, and write the final answer in terms of $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{5}{3x+6}\,\text{d}x & =5\int \frac{1}{3x+6}\,\text{d}x \\  & =5\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot (\frac{1}{3})\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{5}{3}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{5}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =\frac{5}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|3x+6|+C\end{aligned}
$$

We can further simplify the above by writing $C=\frac{5}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡K$ for another arbitrary constant $K,$ and then we can combine the two terms using the laws of logarithms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|3x+6|+C & =\frac{5}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|3x+6|+\frac{5}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡K \\  & =\frac{5}{3}(\operatorname{ln}⁡|3x+6|+\operatorname{ln}⁡K) \\  & =\frac{5}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|3x+6|)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we finally conclude that

$$
\int \frac{5}{3x+6}\,\text{d}x=\frac{5}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|3x+6|).
$$
